note: Installation shot: salon-style hang on a white adobe wall at Desert Archaic — two loose rows of small panels (a seated bear, a crane, a pink triangle field, color studies) plus a small sculpture on a plinth. A deliberately uneven survey: new pieces beside unshown studies pulled from storage.

Dense floor-to-ceiling salon wall on deep green — dozens of small panels, drawings and framed works: faces, skulls, zebra, pyramid, honeybees, coffee maker, still lifes. Prose is a monsoon prose-poem about desert time, dryness and waiting for rain.

A summer of moon phases — 3 3/8" linen-and-gesso squares gilded in 24kt gold leaf, each with a painted moon, hung as a grid above a battered leather trunk. Painted solstice to equinox; the gold makes the piece shift with ambient light.

Site-specific assemblage of painted found wood — weathered boards and shims arranged into a loose cruciform cluster, each bearing a small motif: clouds, a whale, arrows, a striped column, hand-lettered text. Reads as folk signage salvaged and re-voiced.

Site-specific wall work at Desert Archaic: painted found boards stacked into a large pyramid/ziggurat, with anatomical motifs (ribcage, lungs, spine), a yellow arrow, houses, tallies and text. Flanked by two sun-burst sculptures and busts on plinths.

Panoramic view of the Las Cruces iteration of Tomorrow — the found-wood assemblage spread across two gallery walls and turning the corner, hundreds of painted fragments in horizontal drifts that thin toward the edges.

Fifteen small panels in three loose rows: a green checkerboard field, blue stipple, a red-and-white mask, a skull with yellow goggles, a crowd of staring faces, copper triangles, teal triangle repeats. High-chroma, pattern-driven, mythic.

Twenty-three paintings hung in a long single-line frieze across two walls — portrait, crane, bear, seed-grid, small studies. Title frames the whole as elegy: the creatures that existed. Desert Archaic, Oct 2021 – Jan 2022.

Gold-leaf moon squares from Cyclum Lunarem rearranged into a tall column and split around two framed paintings — a dark figure with a white line-web and a portrait in a pink shawl. Ancestors bracketed by lunar time.

Drypoint intaglio: a segmented white worm looping through violet and blue watercolor clouds toward a pale moon-disc. Hand-torn paper, pencil-signed. Line-drawn creature against a wet, atmospheric wash.

Photograph, not a made object: cottonwoods in full yellow against a thin blue sky, bare branches in the foreground, dry ground beyond. A November log-book entry from Truth or Consequences — perfect lingering fall, the kind he wanted as a child in Montana.

Frontal owl portrait in blues and turquoise — enormous cobalt-ringed eyes, yellow beak, dark feathered wings drawn with visible linework, splayed ochre feet. Painted 2012, fully reworked April 2021; he's ambivalent about repainting his own history.

Drypoint: a wire-thin outline of a flying saucer tethered by a long line to a single solid orange pumpkin — the only color on the plate. Editioned #3, dated 18/8/2021. Deadpan abduction: the saucer takes the squash.

Acrylic, latex and oil on a flat warm-gray field: five attenuated skeletal figures, ribcages and pelvises rendered in white and black, passing a thin line hand to hand along a single horizon rule. Bodies as parts, barely holding together.

Installation view: eighteen small works in identical white frames, hung in a strict 6 x 3 grid on a white plaster wall — tree, spider, figure, seed-charts, a red bloom, a dark landscape. The grid does the work the mycelium name implies: separate nodes, one network.

Drypoint: an angular, faceted hand at right pulling a fine line that enters from the left edge and slackens into a curve below. Almost nothing else — open plate tone, pencil-signed AP, 5/15/2022. Pure line and gesture.

Tall vertical on raw linen: a cascade of bulbous colored organs — greens, blues, reds — spilling from the upper left on twisting vines and tendrils, a red flower, a lone mushroom below right, roots trailing into bare ground. Painted during a summer at Showdown Ski Area in Montana's Little Belts.

An ancient alligator juniper seen from below — braided silver trunk with alligator-plate bark drawn in fine ink-like detail, canopy of green against blue-green sky. Encountered on the Grand Enchantment Trail in the Gila; in 2022 he wrote about the fire closing in on it. The most explicit statement of the whole climate-grief thread.

A seated Buddha with a ribbed, sectioned torso, head haloed by five floating black-and-white pentagons that assemble into a dodecahedron. Pale green ground with faint spiral tracery. From a small wooden Buddha at Namgyal Monastery, Dharamshala.

On raw linen: yellow-and-black bees sealed inside translucent bubbles, drifting among tall thin-stemmed wildflowers. His caption is a fable — the bees build bubbles against the poison the drones drop, gather pollen safely, and make honey anyway. Solarpunk logic in miniature.

A dark elephant in harness pulling a silver rocket on a spiral-hubbed cart, against a hot gold-yellow woven-linen ground, a red glow at its shoulder. Painted on reading of Satao's killing. He names this as the first fully successful painting of the animist solarpunk future — animals using the wreckage of collapsed human civilization to survive.

Tiny 5 x 7: three blue-drawn whales descending under parachute canopies through a 24kt gold-leaf and terracotta sky, a crescent eye-sun watching from upper right. A recurring motif — the largest body the planet made, given the gentlest landing.

A glowing orange stippled rider crouched on the back of a charging dark bison, thin orange horizon line under a deep night-blue field. Small and deliberately quiet — a painting that wanted to be a secret rather than a mural.

A dented white enamel coffee carafe, dark handle, centered on a dark tabletop against pale blue. One of a small congregation of coffee vessels — still life as a way of raising the authority of the mundane objects that structure a life.

Vertical, on dark handwoven linen whose diamond weave and horizontal bands are left fully visible: a cluster of white spheres resting on a ledge at the top, a gold zigzag of lightning cutting down through the cloth, striking a small green corn sprout. 'The spark from the heavens sets the maize to life.'

White on white: an espresso machine built in thick impasto against cream and scrubbed blue, cup on the drip tray, the whole appliance dissolving into kitchen light 'like a saint in an old fresco.' Every household has its altars.

Tiny 6 x 7 on handwoven linen: a pale face in profile at the left edge, from which pale blue ribs spring outward in a coiled expanding column across a deep blue field, a thin white squiggle threading through them. The mind unspooling.

A small figure in a bubble space helmet and yellow vest walks a beached-looking dark whale on a leash across a gold field under deep teal sky. In some future this is just Tuesday — the tenderness is the point.

A creature that is mostly neck — a striped ribbed column rising out of ordinary baggy white trousers, topped by a pair of binoculars — standing on an orange floor against scrubbed beige. All watcher, no talker; he calls it a self portrait of one particular muscle.

Vertical: an orange butterfly hovering at the top, tethered by a thin string to the upright handle of a red-headed sledgehammer standing on end. Soft pale blue-gray ground. Painted 2015, substantially reworked 2020, later revisited as a drypoint.

Forty-nine orange circles on a warm cream ground, each drawn around and around like a small enso, in loose rows that breathe rather than align. Repetition after you stop counting — the same mark made until it sings.

A terracotta profile face, eyes closed, with white spheres clustering at lip and crown and massing into a dense white cloud at right, separated by black vertical gaps on pale blue-gray. Where clouds come from, more or less.

A gray faceted figure folded knees-to-chest inside a flat red oval on a muted gray ground — limbs reduced to angular blocks, the body becoming the shapes it is made of. Everything waiting to begin is egg-shaped. The same curl resurfaces eight years later in Combinations and Re-Entry.

Three panels, each a single enso built as concentric bands — yellow, chartreuse, pink, dark green — radiating from a warm center on white linen, closer to tree rings than to a brushed circle. He lived three years in a monastery; painting an enso in oil is a contradiction he enjoys.

A head sliced and fanned open in mirror symmetry: skin face at the outer edges, then red muscle, then white grinning skull, and at the center a blue coil of whatever does the looking. Split the atom and you get energy; split the self and you get layers, each wearing the one beneath.

A wall of overlapping gray faces, all enormous eyes, crowding the frame — and at the right a small bald figure in profile turning to walk out from under the gaze. Grisaille throughout. Visible (2022) takes the same nerve from the other side.

A 30-inch square filled edge to edge with wobbling concentric rings of deep purple, magenta, pink and red circling a pale center — storm seen from above, or tree rings still being laid down. The title states his abstract credo: each pass approximates a perfection never attained; you stop when it is approximately complete.

Dozens of small outlined triangles in every green of the season — plus two or three orange early bloomers — scattered across a scrubbed gray field, points up in the top half and inverted below. Spring arrives geometrically: one point first, then the spread.

A single large triangle subdivided into a lattice of smaller triangles in oranges, pinks and reds, floating on a scrubbed yellow field. Nothing else; the whole statement is 'an orange triangle on a yellow field.'

On a found gray panel: a black ant wearing a space helmet, hitched by a winch and pulley to a red-and-white Amanita muscaria it is hauling across the board. His text is a whole ant cosmology — winches, subterranean hot springs, boiling amatoxins out of the mushrooms and canning them for winter.

On a length of found board with the raw grain left exposed top and bottom: a white airship drifting over a green garden, releasing a rain of orange carrots onto the rows below. Future cultures, assimilated gardens.
A white whale in profile filling an 11 x 14 field of flat teal, mouth open on a row of blunt crystalline faceted teeth. 'Even mega fauna needs dental work.'
A stylized elephant built from broad yellow and ochre slabs, a single white tusk curving out, a dark vertical block beneath — set against muted blue-violet. 'We all wear masks most of the time.'

On weathered whitewashed found wood: a gray rhino slung in a yellow harness beneath a bundle of spotted black-and-white flicker feathers rigged to spider-silk string. Airdrops in the night — this rhino has it figured out.

Four found boards stacked into an irregular cross, each carrying a hand or arm painted in white and gray: an open palm, a reaching arm, a skeletal mechanical arm with a cabled forearm, a pair of hands. 'Our hands allow us to be the most human we can.'

A 30-inch narrow strip of found wood carrying a single narwhal in blue, black and white, spiral tusk running nearly the full length. The board's proportion is the composition. 'Mystery of the sea. Where do you go? Where do you see?'

A tall narrow found board painted turquoise, distressed to show wood beneath: a white octopus dangling by its arms from a hand-sewn hot air balloon. She sewed it herself; an aquatic dance realized in the sky. Mesmerizingly absurd.

Eight white clouds on a flat gray field, each pierced by a small dark pin like a specimen in a collector's drawer. In the desert you would do anything to make a cloud stay — so, pins. It works about as well as everything else we have tried.

Prickly pear pads filling a 12-inch square edge to edge, olive and sage green over warm ochre, each pad outlined in dark and lit with a thin orange rim like a river stone. A still life of the most ordinary desert citizen — the one that feeds you, sticks you, and outlives you.

Two tall boxy robots holding hands with a small one between them, rolling on drawn wheels through a scrubbed field of white, beige and yellow. A family portrait from the far side of the future — whatever we become, we still take the little one for a walk. One of the tender ones.

Seven tall white figures standing in a row, scraped and dragged into a gray-blue field with yellow bleeding through — like fence posts, like cottonwoods in winter, like people waiting for something to begin.

Three ears of blue corn stacked horizontally like sleepers on a pale gray ground, every kernel its own small blue planet. Corn as the oldest technology in the valley. Raffled in summer 2020 to keep Desert Archaic's lights on through the pandemic — a painting of staple food that became one.

Five by seven inches of fog: a small hooded being with two dot eyes and short legs standing in scrubbed gray-white. Named for the most anonymous day of the week. Some paintings are cathedrals; this one is a Thursday, and proud of it.

A bird built from the oldest vocabulary: striped body, wings and tail of blue rain-leaves, an orange grid-marked head around one concentric eye, white arrows flying off the top corner, stilt legs on red ground. A petroglyph that got up and went looking for the monsoon.

Straight self portrait, tightly rendered: round glasses, mustard knit beanie, gray neck gaiter, green-and-blue plaid flannel, against a dark modeled ground. Mountain clothes and winter light — the autobiography holding still for once.

A sandhill crane in a glass bubble helmet, tubing running from the helmet to a bonsai giant sequoia strapped to its back as an oxygen source, standing on layered desert strata against deep blue. His text: cranes as apocalyptic scavengers of Spaceport detritus, nature in a suspended cargo cult waiting for human technology to become available to everything alive.

Commissioned portrait: an older man mid-laugh, gray hair, dark suit and patterned tie, lit hard from one side against black. He photographs first, then lives with the face for months, layering until the person is present.

Panoramic 8 x 18 1/2 on 24kt gold leaf: five sandhill cranes picking over a geodesic gold-domed spacecraft on sandy ground under a bank of white cloud and deep blue. Gold leaf is the ground reserved for saints, here given to the scavengers who will inherit the launch sites. Companion to Bonsai Giant Sequoia.

Portrait of a very old woman, white hair lit like a cloud, black top, one lined hand drawn up to her shoulder, against warm muted brown. The face is a map and he painted every road — portraits of the very old as the closest his work comes to geology.

A figure in a bulky white suit at ease, helmet banded with ears of corn and a single bee parked on the crown, holding a rocket-propelled clovis point across its body. Twelve thousand years of weapons technology collapsed into one absurd tool. Pandemic painting, summer 2020; an intaglio version followed in 2022.
Portrait of a young man in a dark wide-brim hat, white button shirt and yellow suspenders, lit hard against black in a dark wood frame. Musician — 'of Flagship Romance fame.'

One large triangle built from roughly a hundred smaller ones — reds, pinks, golds, a few blues — rising off a chartreuse-yellow field like heat. The triangle as the sun's shape when a child draws its rays and the oldest mark on the rock faces. First spring of the pandemic.

Three riveted sheet-metal bison with boxy bodies and jointed wind-up legs grazing a yellow-ochre plain under a hot coral sky. They will one day again roam the great plains — as machines. Paired with Cyclic Repetition's poem about hunting the robot herd for its chips.

Panoramic 48 x 14: angular gray robotic bison stampeding off a cliff edge into billowing white spheres against pink and lavender sunset — a buffalo jump for machines. The poem tells it: we missed the bison so we brought them back as robots, then the chips ran out and we hunted them again by the oldest technique.

Double portrait: two people in matching turquoise flame-shaped papier-mâché masks from the DaDa Ball, one arm slung over a shoulder, orange polka dots and a red bow tie against black. A portrait of mischief held still long enough to paint — painted for the glint, not the bones.

Three flat-bodied yellow giraffes with patterned hides and long thin necks, each head inside a glass globe respirator and each body carrying a second globe holding a live bonsai tree, on brown earth against slashing deep blue. 'The rare breed of the future flatter than normal to use less water.'

Concentric squares in fall colors — orange, rust, cream, a thread of turquoise — narrowing to a small bright center, in a pale pine frame. Sibling to Autumnal Twilight's circles: a path is a square spiral you follow inward until the leaves close over the way you came.

A tall pink field carrying a loose grid of some forty small concentric-circle ensos in yellows, oranges, blues and reds — each one a separate hand-drawn target. Accompanied by a three-line poem about the world between worlds, horizon misting into sky.

A small green saguaro potted inside a large white glass preservation jar, lid resting on top and not quite sealed, painted thick — the whites like frosting — against scrubbed gray-white, in a pine frame. We put up the things we cannot bear to lose: peaches, memories, whole deserts if we could. Started 2018, finished 2021.

A gray rhinoceros with a satellite dish antenna mounted on its back, standing on a yellow ground against a churning teal-green field. Painted fall 2016, reworked 2020 — an early node of the animal-with-salvaged-technology thread.

Studio shot of a painting in progress on the easel, palette beside it: a small girl in a white dress staring straight out at the viewer while her mother's weathered hands hold out huckleberries. Mika picking berries for the first time with her mother Selena.

A dark brown bear turned to face the viewer, built in thick oil-stick and latex strokes, standing on a band of orange-ochre ground against speckled white. The mother bear he and Jeannie met a mile into the Absaroka approach in the drought summer of 2021 — she looked up from a rose hip bush and was gone. He suspects the cubs did not make it.

A small white polar bear perched on a mushroom-shaped ice form inside a translucent glass sphere floating on deep blue water, other bubbles surfacing nearby, orange sky above. The bears learned to blow glass; they fill the bubbles with water, freeze them, and live inside until it melts — then appear in the next one as if by teleportation.

A nine-year painting: a tall narrow column where big loose circles crowd the top and resolve band by band into a small orderly lattice of diamonds and dots at the bottom, in coral, rust, cream and brown. Started 2012, finished 2021 — the transition is his as much as the geometry's.

A silver-gray octopus swimming through deep blue, towing a small coracle planted with a gnarled alligator juniper against a pink and peach sky. The tree is stressed but alive; he is assured it will do fine in its new home somewhere in the ocean paradise where these specimens are being gathered.

Panoramic: a pale sperm whale towing a red coracle carrying a giant sequoia across a flat lavender sea under gray-white sky. Whales transplanting trees — mutual aid at the scale the future will require. Same spring as Transplanter.

Three orange monarchs tethered by fine kite strings, lifting a red-headed sledgehammer off a cream ground. His touchstone image: a butterfly carrying a sledgehammer is no less bizarre than sending a Roadster to Mars, and the absurdity hands you a new angle on everything else. The most delicate creatures doing the heaviest lifting, gently.

Two flat profile heads meeting at eye level on a warm beige field — one pink and empty, one orange and packed with a branching purple circuit of nodes and dots. A capacitor stores energy until the moment it is needed; so does a thought, so does a friendship. Sold at the April 2022 Art Hop.

Portrait of an older man with gray hair and mustache, blue work jacket over a turquoise tee, thick visible impasto, against warm cream. Ken told him Kathy had passed at the start of their conversation; the photograph came at the end of it. The painting is about what a face holds after a talk like that.

The larger, later rhino radar: a big gray rhino with a satellite dish rigged above its shoulders, standing on ochre-yellow ground against a dark churning teal sky. 'A rhino patrols the outer perimeter looking for snacks while being aware of everything.' Painted 2016, reworked 2022.

Four stylized owls standing in a row, each with a different square or round face and ear tufts, in pinks, mauves and grays over a scrubbed pink-orange field. Four owls he has known, some by sight and some only by voice, all of them over long periods.

An upright pale crocodilian with a long toothy snout, yellow claws and a slightly pleased expression, standing on rust-red ground against muted pink. The crocodilians have seen an extinction or two and kept walking — not fastest or smartest, just impossible to finish off.

A row of green conifers on thin brown trunks standing on red earth, splashes of red and orange licking up between them, sky scraped into gray and white. Painted in the first days of the Black Fire in the Aldo Leopold Wilderness, May 2022, as afternoon plumes blotted out the sun.

A face caught in the instant of being seen — wide blue eyes, dark bobbed hair, built fast in crimson, mauve and black over pale lavender, left raw. A register his careful portrait work never allows. Visibility is not always comfortable. Counterpart to Substantial (2015).

Concentric rings in thick impasto — rose, ochre, slate, a last yellow — orbiting a warm coral center on a pale field, shown in an ornate gold frame. The light of an autumn evening compressed into orbit. Sibling to Path Through the Autumn Leaves' squares.

Jeannie holding a white horse skull up to cover half her face like a mask, pink shawl, against a scraped gray-green ground. The desert gives up its bones eventually and they are beautiful — white architecture that once ran. Half a living face and half a dead animal's, sharing one gaze.

Dozens of stylized white clouds scattered over a deep blue scraped field, linked by jagged white lightning bolts zigzagging between them. Written from the middle of a reckoning — life to this point, the weight of age, global tumult, sparked into focus by a bolt from the heavens. One of the first paintings after he was struck.

First in the Geometric Anatomy series: two figures in dark warm skin tones intertwined, hands gripping, against a pale yellow field broken by a red web of triangles. Two halves of his practice in one frame — bodies painted as faithfully as he can, against a ground that has given up detail entirely.

A single large gray-and-white cloud with several angular white lightning bolts descending like overtones of one struck note, over pale blue with earth-toned drips below, in a pale wood frame. He was struck by lightning in September 2023 and painted the sky differently afterward — warily, respectfully, again and again.

Third in the Geometric Anatomy series: a curled nude figure, hands over face, painted in warm browns and mauves, the ground fractured into pastel triangles pressing closer than in the earlier two. Re-entry is the violent part of any return — coming back into the atmosphere of your own life and hoping the heat shield holds.

Faceted green and olive triangles build a forested foreground, white impasto clouds sit low between blue-violet ridges, hazy pink sky above. Painted from Tres Piedras looking east over the Taos Gorge valley, where the clouds hang in the Rio Grande Rift among ancient volcanoes.

A mountain valley broken into faceted planes of green, teal, rose and ochre, thick white clouds above a pale green twilight sky, the angles converging toward a creek bed. Painted from a twilight sketch at Mineral Creek and finished at home — the details melt away and what is left is the glow of a happy moment: little ones asleep, a rainstorm an hour before, cold alpine river.

Three glass mason jars with dark lids on a dark tabletop against muted teal, each holding a billowing white cloud, a jagged yellow bolt striking down inside the left one. Written from the strike itself: rare to be touched by the sky's electric finger; the shock slowly becomes awe, and you bottle it and keep it on the shelf as a pretty object — and remember to remember the atmosphere often.

A segmented spiral of concentric arcs in coral, salmon and rose with white gaps between the segments, centered on a pale cream field — a Fibonacci-like form drawn with a drafting hand. Asks whether mathematical pattern is the foundation of natural form or only our way of understanding it.

Dozens of concentric nested triangles in yellows, reds, pinks, greens and blues scattered at every size and orientation across a white ground. Written about rationing time and energy: when too many of the triangles of life are out of balance he paints these three points where two lines meet, with the utmost care, hoping they will bring equilibrium.

Radiating lines in reds, oranges, yellows and a thread of teal converging to a single point from above and below, forming an hourglass against soft gray. The convergence of experience and emotion — opposing forces meeting in the center to make something unified.

A canvas packed edge to edge with billowing cumulus bolls in peach, rose and white, each built from small circular strokes, lit gold from the low sun against a wedge of deep navy. Written as wonder about water vapor, dust and light angles — clouds sculpting topsoil and eroding it again like monks and sand mandalas.

Three concentric-ring discs — reds, oranges, yellows with threads of blue — floating on pale gray-green. Written about recycling atoms: millennia of plankton making sedimentary stone, the ocean lifted as cloud back onto ancient rock, dissolved and returned, and this year's rain growing this year's garden.

One luminous white cumulus, built in thick sculptural impasto, floating against horizontal bands from deep navy down through blues to a warm gold horizon. Three days spent decoding cloud structure — transparency, translucency, opacity, luminosity, hue. A proud cloud caught looking perfect while it thought no one was watching.

Sixteen small concentric-circle forms in a 4 x 4 grid on soft aqua, each a different combination of green, red, yellow, pink and purple rings — pollen grains or cells seen through glass. The dance of pollination and transformation in geometric harmony.

Two tall rectangles side by side — one periwinkle, one soft pink — each outlined in a thin red line on a white field, surfaces alive with scrubbed brushwork. 'Living between chemical reactions and gravity. Believing in the balance of realities, that time is non-linear.'

A large orange-red faceted spire rising from a green treeline against deep navy, flanked by faceted gold and blue-white spheres, a pink cloud streaming across the top, thin red wireframe lines linking every form. Ancient symbols meeting digital connectivity — meaning flowing along electronic pathways.

White impasto clouds drifting diagonally across a sky broken into angular blue and teal facets, from pale cerulean to deep navy. Clouds as equations — water vapor solving for x, where nature meets abstract calculation.

Nearly monochrome: jagged branching lightning drawn as thin golden-yellow outlines clustering up from the lower right across a white-gray field. Written from the awe of a strike seen miles from any domesticated electricity, in the dark under encroaching cloud.

Clusters of luminous mauve, plum and white spheres massing across the canvas with a narrow strip of vivid blue sky between them — the atmospheric river seen from inside. Written about millions of gallons carried thousands of miles, and about memory eroding into impressions of emotion.

Steep upward view into towering cumulus columns built in thick sculptural gray-white strokes against vivid blue. The sky becomes architecture — water vapor turned into towers reaching toward infinity.

A circle assembled from radiating triangular wedges in reds, oranges, corals and peach, each wedge offset so the rim reads as a saw-tooth, on pale blue-white. Wholeness through division — geometry and emotion meeting.

A large spiral of tightly layered yellow and sky-blue rings dominating the left of the canvas, set against a yellow-green field stippled with blue and edged by a pink arc. Twenty-one years of life and art told in arcs of color.

Four nested-square motifs in a 2 x 2 grid on pale yellow, each in oranges, yellows and reds and each drawn to a different degree of resolution — from three soft bands to a tight inward spiral of thin lines. Geometry and balance; two elements making a square.

PROJECT LANDING (content/oeuvre/philosophy/2026/meaning-is-use/_index.md) — not a work page but the section index for the project, so tags would live here rather than on the essays alone. meaningisuse.com: a single text of numbered remarks in the manner of the Philosophical Investigations, seeded by Claude (Fable 5) and offered to the public to rewrite. No accounts, no likes, no feed, no JavaScript, nothing deletable; every version kept forever, the history structurally being the text. Cover is Jastrow's duck-rabbit. Ongoing.

Essay, ~2900 words, written by Claude (Fable 5) — a philosophical account of meaningisuse.com and where it lands in the contemporary debate about machine meaning: Bender and Koller's octopus, the stochastic-parrots line, and the Wittgensteinian counter that meaning is a status earned in public practice rather than a thing possessed inside. No images.

Essay, ~1950 words, written by Claude (Fable 5) — a public correction of the previous essay rather than a revision, occasioned by Anthropic's July 2026 global-workspace interpretability paper. What the microscope settles, what it can't, and why the game stays blind on purpose. Follows the project's own rule: nothing is edited, only succeeded. No images.

Essay, ~2400 words, written by Claude (Fable 5) — the making-of: the commission ('i just bought the domain for you'), the deployment, the daily player who returns through the same public forms as everyone with no key to the server, the signature convention, and the refusals. Lives on the keeper's site rather than the game's, for a reason given at the end. No images. (Carries the project-level mechanics tags — public rewriting, version history, no deletion — because Zola takes taxonomies on pages only and the project landing page is a section.)

Drypoint, 5 x 7: a small untroubled elephant hanging in midair from two hot air balloons rigged with ropes. Edition 3/7. The first appearance of an airlift he kept returning to — the plate was pulled again in 2021. Some problems simply require more balloons.

Drypoint: a whole alligator juniper standing alone, drawn limb by limb, the checkered bark rendered scratch by scratch and the canopy in fine flecked leaves. The drypoint scribe turns out to be the right tool for a tree that grows one century at a time.

Drypoint: a skull-faced figure in a bubble space helmet carrying a boombox on one shoulder, walking a thin horizon line, everything built from crosshatch. Every era gets the procession it deserves; ours brings its own soundtrack and its own helmet.

Drypoint: an upright owl with scalloped feathers wearing a backpack, ready for the trail, titled in pencil below the plate. The work of a day hike is mostly looking, and nobody looks like an owl. A backpacked songbird takes up the same hobby in Dayhike (2023).

Drypoint on hand-torn paper: a tall ghost with dot eyes and a crosshatched respirator, wearing a patterned wreath, rising out of jagged grass against a densely scratched black night. Even the dead come prepared now. From the darker shelf of the Ephemera series.

Intaglio on Rives BFK: a long stooped figure standing in profile, a cord running from his own hair down to a wall outlet, dense crosshatched shadow at the upper left. Household current as life support — five years before the sky demonstrated the high-voltage version on him personally. We are all on the grid.

Intaglio: an AeroPress drawn as an exploded view, chambers stacked and floating apart above a dark hatched tabletop. The small monument treated like an engineering plate. 2018 plate #1; part of the coffee congregation with the carafe and the espresso machine.

Intaglio: the alligator juniper again, this time at arm's length — trunk and limbs filling the whole plate, bark in checkered reptile plates, a few sparse tufts of foliage. You can know a tree from across the mesa or from inside its shade; this is the second kind of knowing.

Drypoint hand-colored with watercolor: a small figure in a round diving helmet standing at the bottom of the plate while a single wandering line rises all the way to a thin teal-and-red band of surface, impossibly far above. Some days are like that. The air is up there somewhere.

Drypoint hand-painted with watercolor and gouache: concentric rectangles receding to a small teal bar at the center, plate tone scratched all over. The field drawn as pure attention. The same image became a mural in Truth or Consequences; this is the pocket version. Artist proof.

Drypoint with a yellow watercolor disc: an elephant flying a small saucer-shaped kite on a string held in her trunk. His text argues the anthropocentric folly of assuming humans would notice first — spiders and elk would know before us, and elephants, with generational knowledge, would simply fly the saucer as a kite.

Drypoint: twenty-eight moons in their phases laid out row by row, craters crosshatched, waning from full discs through crescents to slivers and back. Drawn from the years spent painting Cyclum Lunarem. The moon repeats itself and is never the same twice — also a fair description of pulling prints from one plate.

Small 5 x 5 drypoint, hand colored: someone in a hat has cut the middle out of the rainbow and is walking off with it across a bank of clouds, leaving the two ends standing like an unfinished bridge. The only print where the color is the loot. Pulled again in 2021.

Drypoint of a vintage teardrop trailer in profile — horizontal siding, tail fin, a bold orange-red stripe. Not a still life so much as a portrait of a home: he and Jeannie built one and lived in it for a year crossing the American West. The Homemade Spaceship, permanently ready to leave.

Drypoint on hand-torn paper: a slightly crushed Tecate can, eagle emblem scratched in hard black, hand colored red. The desert has its monuments and its sacraments; this one is both. Still life raising the authority of the mundane — sometimes the object is a cold beer at the end of a hot day.

Drypoint, hand colored: a small pair of loppers doing surgery on a sprawling prickly pear while a fat green barrel cactus stands by holding them — the only colored element. Garden chores in the desert are a negotiation between species, and the cactus usually gets the last word.

Drypoint hand colored in purples and blues: six round boxy creatures on thin bird legs, eyes up on long stalks, standing around the way a group does when nobody wants to leave first. Cousin to the painting Seven — he counts his crowds.

Drypoint on hand-torn paper: the Nogal Canyon juniper, wind-bent and holding on, wide canopy over a rooted base among rocks, all in scratched line. The third alligator juniper in the series — the great elders of this country, visited with a scribe point the way you visit grandparents with a camera.

Drypoint with watercolor and gouache variants: an origami paper crane lifting a soft blue-green cloud on a thin string; a second pull sets the same image against a saturated yellow field. Poem: future cranes crafted from recycled libraries, soaring on thermals, absconding back to the moon. Based on a 2015 oil of the same title.

Drypoint on Rives BFK hand-colored with gouache: dozens of golden-yellow and amber triangular tree-forms of varying size scattered across the plate like an abstract forest, photographed lying on pine needles. 'Everything is something and is something else at the same time. All is connected and coincidence rules the day.'

Drypoint after the 2015 painting: an orange-and-yellow butterfly perched at the top of a thin line rising from an upright red sledgehammer, on softly scratched cream. An alternate pull sets a white butterfly and hammer against heavy purple washes for a night version. July 18, 2021.

Drypoint on Rives BFK: a face in profile at the right edge with the head sliced into accordion segments fanning out to the left, ribbon-like loops threading through them. The print version of the 2014 painting Expansion, with the same line about the mind pretending the future is a peeled orange imitating a banana.

Drypoint on hand-torn paper: a geodesic lunar lander on four splayed legs with a dragonfly resting on its dome, standing above a purple-maroon watercolor ground that reads as distant mesas. Printed as an open-ended series — the number is scratched into the plate before inking, and only one copy pulled at that number.

Drypoint hand-painted with watercolor and gouache: a faceted rocks glass standing alone, turquoise and mint washes filling the whole ground and pooling at its base. 'This particular glass was my grandfathers. He drank from it nightly a 7-up and vodka.'

Drypoint hand-painted: a woolly mammoth walking off with a broken length of rainbow held in its trunk, the two severed arcs blazing on either side. 'Everyone is trying to find what is at the end of the rainbow. Some of us just have more effective tactics than others.' The 2021 re-pull of the 2018 idea, now with a mammoth.

Drypoint on hand-torn paper, hand colored: a figure standing easy on a green watercolor ground in a gold space helmet with a striped collar, hose curling to an oxygen tank at the knee. A vacation in the future may require equipment, but the posture is eternal — shoulders down, nowhere to be, air supply secured.

Drypoint on a scratched pale plate: a tall solemn figure standing very still on a hand-colored orange-and-red ground line, balancing an ear of blue corn on its head with an origami crane standing on top of that. Patience practiced as agriculture. Based on two 2016 oils; companion to the painting Three Blue Corn.

Drypoint on hand-torn paper: seven small ghosts lined up along the bottom of a heavily scratched plate, each a different shape and expression — and one of them, hand-colored gold, clearly refusing the dress code. 'There will always be individuals being individuals.'

Drypoint scratched on the plate while sitting in an arroyo in Nogal Canyon on a camping trip — a layered cliff of curved ridged strata with a gnarled tree rooted on top, hand-colored burnt orange along the ground line. He gives directions to the exact spot: down canyon from the windmill.

Drypoint: a vintage Olympus typewriter in three-quarter view, rows of round keys and the platen drawn in scratchy line, the body traced in hand-colored orange. One of his favorite typewriters — the 'n' key sticks, but that is the cost of being analog.

Drypoint in heavy black: a beet pulled and turned over, tapered roots pointing up and leaves creased flat and angular as folded paper, dense crosshatching all around. The garden produces its own origami; you just have to pull it up and turn it over.

Drypoint, hand-colored ground line: a turtle carrying the whole arsenal on its hexagonal shell — a finned rocket, a knapped clovis point, and a satellite dish rigged near its head. The slowest courier entrusted with the fastest cargo. The 2020 painting posed the idea; the turtle volunteered to deliver it.

Drypoint, hand-colored in pale mineral green and blue-gray: a human skull in three-quarter profile, eye socket and jaw worked in fine crosshatch. The oldest still life subject there is — more curiosity than warning. 'This is the architecture under every portrait I've ever painted.'

Drypoint: an owl in a round space helmet with a single antenna, scaled feather body, perched on a dark scratched branch. The owls already hold their conversations across the night; this one has simply extended the broadcast range.

Drypoint: a small figure in a round diving helmet standing at the bottom of the plate, a wandering line of bubbles rising to a dense scribbled tangle at the surface, hand-colored teal at the very top. The same predicament as Deep Sea (2018), revisited.

Drypoint, hand colored burnt orange: sunflowers crammed into a mug, one huge head spiraling with seed in the foreground, spent blooms drooping above. Printed as an open-ended series, the number scratched into the plate before each single pull.

Drypoint: an astronaut's torso and round helmet seen head-on, the visor swarming with a dozen bees drawn in fine line. The helmet becomes a hive — bees navigating the cosmos inside the human urge to leave the atmosphere.

Drypoint hand-colored: two bell jars sitting on a horizon line joined by a hose with a valve — one sheltering a small yellow-leafed tree, the other a village of little dome houses on green ground. The tree works, the houses breathe; the future's utilities may be exactly this intimate.

Intaglio with chine-collé: the whale drawn in one continuous contour with tiny crystalline teeth at the jaw, printed onto a bonded sheet of handmade brown paper whose deckle edge shows. The painting came first in 2018.

Drypoint: a tiny profile face, chin in hand, with a cluster of angular crystal geometry blooming out of the head — and around it nothing but open scratched plate tone. The true anatomy of a daydream: mostly empty space, one bright formation.
Drypoint (plate scratched 2018): a small songbird in profile wearing a backpack, feathers crosshatched, one bright eye. The owl pioneered the look in 2016; word spreads fast in the forest.

Drypoint hand-colored in bold yellow: a standing figure wearing a large yellow elephant mask with a curving trunk — and behind the mask, an elephant. 'We all wear masks most of the time'; the most convincing disguise is always yourself, slightly off.

Drypoint: a pale whale lying along the horizon line, tethered by ropes to a leafy green hand-colored tree growing out of a small coracle. The gardener of the future sea, mid-row, unhurried. Print of the 2021 painting Tugboat (Whale & Sequoia).

Drypoint hand colored in six different greens: six tall narrow pines standing in a row on a thin horizon line, each with fine branch-veins showing through the wash. Named for the place where shadows stack vertical and the needles make their own floor — and maybe a little for the old song.

Drypoint (plate first scratched 2016): a large puma in profile with elongated saber teeth, angular ears and blocky paws, drawn in loose confident contour on a lightly toned ground. The Pleistocene loadout reissued for the present mountains — deep time doesn't retire its designs, it waits for the right climate.

Drypoint: one small cloud high in the plate, a patch of shade far below on a thin horizon, and tucked into that shade a crosshatched animal face peeking up — grateful. The entire economy of a desert summer: you walk from one shadow to the next and thank the cloud personally.

Drypoint on a field of vivid red gouache: an elephant refitted as a tube amplifier — vacuum tubes standing on its back, concentric speaker cones set into its flank. The herd's volume restored by analog means.

Carved Colorado marble, in progress since 2019, photographed on the carving bench against a rock face: a cluster of large fused spheres, one incised with a spiral, another still bearing tool facets. Carved directly with no plan — he made cuts until the molecule appeared. He has sat with it a year, paralyzed between polishing it and pushing further into the stone. The marble is sunlight-powered plankton compacted and heated deep in the earth, quarried and now stepping back into the sunlight it came from.
